L141.question: When the lake holder announces that the target is evil or good, how often is the target really on that side? Split by first / second / third lake and by the holder's own side.
method: Recomputed every day by generate_cache.py (compute_lake_claim_feature) from every game log in the spreadsheet: this time {{games}} games and {{links}} lake checks, data as of {{date}}.

A lake check is a line "H>T x" in the text record: H is the holder's seat, T the target's seat (0 means seat 10), a trailing x = announced evil, o = announced good, nothing (or ?) = no announcement. Only the first three lake lines of a game count, as the first, second and third lake.
Sides come from the game's role sheet: Assassin, Morgana, Mordred and Oberon are evil, every other role is good.
Reliability = announcements that match the target's real side ÷ announcements in the cell (n).
"By holder" pools the three lakes and splits them by the holder's own side into four cells.
95% intervals are Wilson score intervals (z = 1.96) from the cache; cells with n < {{min}} are flagged as small samples.
Lake lines with no announcement ({{undeclared}} this time) are left out of every cell but counted in the total.
read: "Said evil {{exRate}}% [{{exLo}}–{{exHi}}] n={{exN}}" means: of the {{exN}} times a {{exLakeEn}} holder said evil, the target really was evil {{exRate}}% of the time; the true rate is roughly between {{exLo}}% and {{exHi}}%.

Check the holder's side first: good holders almost always tell the truth; only part of an evil holder's announcements are true, and an evil holder calling someone evil is usually framing a good player (see "By holder").

The per-lake numbers mix good and evil holders: the more evil holders, the lower the overall reliability. Differences between lakes mostly reflect who holds the lake, not a person changing how they announce.
caveats: The Lady of the Lake shows the holder the target's real side, so an announcement that does not match is almost always a lie; a few may be typos in the record.
By the rules the next holder is the previous target, so second and third holders are in effect chosen by the previous holder, and their good / evil mix differs from the first lake.
Game logs are typed by hand: a missing mark is left out, a wrong mark is counted.
These are averages over all players, not any one player; individual habits can differ a lot.

L142.question: After announcing a lake result, does the holder pick teams that match the announcement when they lead? Does the consistency rate differ by role?
method: One-off study: the original report {{source}} lives on the owner's PC, not in the repository; scripts/build_feature_studies.py wrote its numbers into the cache: a {{games}}-game snapshot, {{links}} lake checks, {{leaderEvents}} teams picked by a holder who had announced a lake result.
The daily update does not recompute these numbers; generate_cache.py (annotate_feature_studies) only rewrites the conclusion from them and flags cells with n < {{min}} as small samples.

One event = one team picked by a holder who had announced; a pick that matches the announcement is "consistent", otherwise "inconsistent" (the report's Section 2 "leader picks alignment"; the typical inconsistency is calling someone evil and then putting them on the team).
Consistency = consistent ÷ (consistent + inconsistent), n = events for the role; the role is the holder's own role.

High-EV cells: among the combinations role × announced evil / good × consistent or not, the {{cellCount}} whose games ended 3-red furthest from the baseline (3-red rate over all games of the snapshot, {{baseline}}%); Δ 3-red = the group's 3-red rate − baseline.
95% intervals are computed by the site: consistency from consistent / total; high-EV cells from the 3-red rate × n back to a count, then the Wilson method (z = 1.96).
read: Read n and the interval first: roles with enough data differ little and their intervals overlap; roles with n < {{min}} (including the 100% cell) have very wide intervals and show no pattern.
An inconsistency is worth a question but does not identify a side on its own.
Treat the high-EV cells as hints only: they are the extremes picked from many cells and will most likely shrink with new data.
caveats: Only holders who later lead produce events; evil holders rarely lead afterwards, so almost every evil role is a small sample.
The high-EV cells are the largest gaps picked from all combinations, mostly with small n: picking extremes exaggerates them (multiple comparisons).
Δ 3-red is a correlation, not a cause: consistency and how the game is going affect each other.
One-off study: the numbers stay at the {{games}}-game snapshot and do not follow the daily update.

L143.question: When the Assassin shoots after 3-blue, is the target related to how often they led or where they sat? Does the chance of hitting Merlin change with that?
method: One-off study: the original report {{source}} is not in the repository; scripts/build_feature_studies.py wrote it into the cache: a {{games}}-game snapshot, {{attempts}} assassinations. The daily update does not recompute the numbers; generate_cache.py only rewrites the conclusion from them.
Hit rate = shots whose target really was Merlin ÷ shots in the group (n); missed = 100% − hit rate.

Leader tiers: shots are split by how many times the target led in that game into most / middle / least (cut points as in the original report; the site cannot verify them); the three tiers add up to {{tierTotal}} shots.
The seat table splits by the target's seat; the cache only keeps the {{seatCount}} seats with the highest hit rate, the others are not provided.
95% intervals are computed by the site from hit rate × n back to a count, then the Wilson method (z = 1.96); n < {{min}} is flagged as a small sample.
read: Hit rate is "how often the Assassin was right when choosing this kind of player", not "how often this kind of player gets chosen".
The most-led tier has a higher hit rate, but check whether the intervals overlap first; and how often someone leads is mostly seat rotation (who starts, how many rounds), not how active they are.
To find Merlin, read what people say and how they vote, not their lead count or seat.
caveats: The seat table lists only the top seats: listing the highest ones overstates the gap, and the seats left out may be about the same (selection bias).
Lead count is tied to seat and game length (longer games give everyone more leads): a confounder.
One-off study: the numbers stay at the {{games}}-game snapshot and do not follow the daily update.

L136.question: After the team changes, do players change their vote (approve to reject or back)? Do good, evil and each role flip at different rates?
method: One-off study: the original report {{source}} is not in the repository; scripts/build_feature_studies.py wrote it into the cache: a {{games}}-game snapshot, {{chances}} vote chances. The daily update does not recompute the numbers; generate_cache.py only rewrites the conclusion from them.
From the study's name: a chance = one player's vote after the team changed, a flip = that vote differs from their vote on the previous team (about {{perPlayerGame}} chances per player per game).
Overall flip rate by side (cache summary): good {{blue}}%, evil {{red}}%, a {{delta}}pp gap.

Each role also has two flip columns (cache fields flipRedPct / flipBluePct, labelled red / blue); how the two are split is only in the original report and the site cannot confirm it, so they are labelled by field name.
signed EV = flip % (blue) − flip % (red) (the cache's numbers check out), in points; the original study reads a positive value as a "good signal".
No interval: a player's several votes in one game are not independent, so the {{chances}} chances cannot be treated as independent samples.
read: Roles' signed EV fall within {{span}}pp; the sides differ by only {{delta}}pp overall.
A player has about {{perPlayerGame}} chances per game, so a {{delta}}pp gap is about {{perGameDiff}} more or fewer flips per game: impossible to tell at the table.
Do not infer a side from a changed vote.
caveats: A "flip" ignores direction and reason (who was swapped in or out); averaging different situations can cancel out.
The sample is large, so such a small gap may be statistically real, but it is of little practical use.
One-off study: the numbers stay at the {{games}}-game snapshot and do not follow the daily update.

L139.question: In games where a round's mission went all the way to the fifth proposal (P5, forced), do the three endings come out differently from other games?
method: One-off study: the original report {{source}} is not in the repository; scripts/build_feature_studies.py wrote it into the cache: a {{games}}-game snapshot. The daily update does not recompute the numbers; generate_cache.py only rewrites the conclusion from them.

P5 = the fifth proposal of a round: when the first four teams are all rejected, the fifth goes on the mission without a vote (forced). "P5 in R3" = games whose third mission went to the fifth proposal.

3-red rate = share of these games that ended 3-red; baseline {{baseline}}% = the 3-red rate over all games of the snapshot. Δ 3-red / Δ 3-blue dead / Δ 3-blue alive = the group's share of that ending − the share over all games (points); the three add up to about 0.
"With / without P5 in R3" splits all games in two: {{withN}} + {{withoutN}} = {{games}} games.

R1 is left out: almost every game reaches P5 in R1, so there is no comparison group (the report attributes it to padding in the spreadsheet import; in this community the first four R1 proposals are also often "talk teams" that never go on a mission).
95% intervals are computed by the site from the 3-red rate × n back to a count, then the Wilson method (z = 1.96); n < {{min}} is flagged as a small sample.
read: This is a conditional rate: among games reaching P5 in R3, 3-red differs from the baseline by {{r3delta}}pp. It only says these games end 3-red at a different frequency, not that reaching P5 makes evil stronger.
R4 and R5 have few games ({{r4n}} and {{r5n}}) and wide intervals: check whether the interval covers the baseline before reading the gap.
caveats: Selection bias: rejecting all the way to P5 is itself the result of a game already tilting evil (good cannot control the table); P5 is a symptom of a bad position, not the cause, and not evidence of evil cover.
One-off study: the numbers stay at the {{games}}-game snapshot and do not follow the daily update.
L139.baselineNow: The {{baseline}}% baseline is the 3-red rate of the study's snapshot; the current cache's 3-red rate over all games is {{currentThreeRed}}% (different snapshot and filters), so the two cannot be subtracted directly.

blocks.missionHint: Missions: 3-Red ÷ all of this group's games (red failed three missions); blue = 3-Blue ÷ all
blocks.assassinationHint: Assassination: only games that reached 3 blue missions, 3-Blue dead ÷ (3-Blue dead + 3-Blue alive), i.e. how often the assassin hit Merlin; n = 3-Blue games (3-Red games have no assassination)
blocks.finalHint: Game result: (3-Red + 3-Blue dead) ÷ all of this group's games; blue win rate = 3-Blue alive ÷ all
blocks.note: All three blocks are from red's side; blue = 100% − red. Missions = 3-Red ÷ all; Assassination = 3-Blue dead ÷ 3-Blue games (3-Red games have no assassination); Game result = (3-Red + 3-Blue dead) ÷ all. The n after each rate is its denominator.
